title: Predecode Adapter + Prefetch: design sketch for tokenizer/runtime boundary
body:
Context and motivation:

We routinely see tokenization as a non-trivial portion of per-request latency in production for short-text traffic and bursty concurrent workloads. The runtime currently treats tokenization as a synchronous CPU-bound step at the request ingress; this couples runtime scheduling, batching and cold-start behaviour with tokenizer cost variability (different models, vocab/merges, normalizers).

This doc sketches an alternative boundary: a lightweight predecode adapter + prefetch caching layer that moves common work off the critical path and exposes a small asynchronous contract between the serving runtime and tokenizer. Goal is reduced tail latency, better batching behavior, and pragmatic cacheability without demanding a full rework of model loaders or tokenizers.

High level idea:

- Predecode adapter: a thin service/bolt inside the runtime process or colocated helper that converts request text into a compact intermediate representation (IR) suitable for fast conversion into model token ids. The IR is intentionally smaller than full token ids and more cache-friendly (e.g., normalized text fingerprint, byte spans, token boundary candidates, and stable tokenizer-version tag).
- Prefetch + persistent key-value cache: cache IR and/or final token ids keyed by a stable key (hash of normalized text + tokenizer-version + model-config). Cache supports both in-memory LRU for hot keys and a backing persisted cache (rocksdb/redis) for cross-process reuse.
- Async handoff and fallback: runtime schedules tokenization work based on SLO/priority and can choose: (a) serve from cache, (b) schedule predecode work to return IR rapidly and continue decoding to tokens in background, (c) fallback to synchronous tokenizer if deadlines are tight.

Why use an IR rather than tokens?

- Token id sets vary by model and quantization; an IR that captures normalization + boundary candidates + tokenizer-version allows cheap conversion to final ids by model-specific fast path. This shrinks cached value sizes and increases cache hit-rate for minor model/merging differences.
- IRs can be merged or chunked for long inputs, enabling reuse of overlapping prefixes.

Proposed boundary contract (sketch):

API: TokenAdapter.request_predecode(request_id: string, text: string, hints: list[string]) -> {status: string, key: string, ir_ready: bool}
- status: ACCEPTED | REJECTED
- key: stable cache key for this text+tokenizer-version
- ir_ready: whether IR is in cache immediately or a background task was scheduled

API: TokenAdapter.get_tokens(key: string, timeout_ms: int) -> {tokens: list[int] | null, partial_ir: blob | null, reason: string}
- If tokens exist in cache return immediately; if not but IR exists return partial_ir (small blob) so runtime can begin constructing request routing/kv-cache checks and continue generation once tokens arrive; if neither, block up to timeout_ms before returning null and runtime must decide to fallback to sync tokenization.

Scheduler heuristics (runtime integration):

- Priority buckets: high-priority (interactive, p95 latency SLO tight), medium (background interactive), low (batch/async inference). High-priority requests prefer cache or sync tokenization to avoid queueing; medium will accept IR-first flow; low will be scheduled to background tokenizers.
- Microbatch-aware tokenization: batch tokenization jobs by first grouping predecode keys that share tokenizer-version + normalization pipeline. Use batching window configurable by priority: high 1–2ms, medium 5–10ms, low 20–50ms.
- Backpressure signals from model queue: if GPU queues are full, proactively predecode to smooth upcoming load.

Cache key and invalidation rules:

- Key schema: sha256(normalized_text) + ":" + tokenizer_version + ":" + model_tokenizer_profile_id
- Normalization pipeline must be deterministic and pinned; any change increments tokenizer_version causing cache misses (design tradeoff: re-tokenization vs correctness).
- Eviction: LRU with size cap + TTL for persisted backing; explicit invalidation when tokenizer_version bump or merge table changes.

IR format (compact, stable, few hundred bytes max):

- normalized_text_fingerprint: 64-bit or 128-bit
- boundary_spans: list of start/end byte offsets (prefer delta-encoded)
- unicode_normalization_tag: string
- tokenizer_version: string
- hints: bitflags (prefer_fast_unicode, preserve_whitespace, allow_split_on_punct)
IR should avoid embedding full token id arrays except when the conversion to token ids is expected to be identical across many model variants (rare).

Conversion fast-paths within runtime:

- IR -> token ids: each model loader should expose a tiny native fast-path that consumes IR and emits ids using table lookups; optimized for CPU vector ops and memory-local vocab.
- If model requires specialized tokenization (custom merges), those loaders register conversion hooks with TokenAdapter on start.

Key metrics to add (suggested names):

- tokenizer.predecode.requests_total
- tokenizer.predecode.cache_hit_ratio
- tokenizer.predecode.ir_return_ms_p50/p95/p99
- tokenizer.tokens_from_ir_ms_p50/p95/p99
- tokenizer.sync_fallback_rate
- tokenizer.batch_size_histogram (when batching predecode jobs)
- tokenizer.memory_cache_bytes

Experiment matrix (initial A/B plan):

- Canary cohort (5% traffic): IR-only path + in-memory cache, measure p95 and p99 latency, CPU utilization, cache hit ratio.
- Middle cohort (20%): enable persistent backing store (local RocksDB) and microbatching window tuning for medium priority traffic.
- Aggressive cohort (50+%): enable predecode for low priority traffic only; measure tail latency changes and cost delta.
Rollout safety and fallback plan:

- Start with read-only mode: token adapter computes IR but runtime always falls back to existing sync tokenizer for actual tokens; compare latencies and IR usefulness offline.
- Next opt-in caching read path: serve tokens from cache only if hit and tokens validated against runtime model mapping.
- Full path enabled per priority bucket with auto-disable if p99 increases beyond threshold or error rates rise.

Open questions / risks:

- Token reuse across models: how often will IR->token conversion produce same ids across model variants? If low, benefits diminish. We mitigate by focusing on IR reuse for prefix-sharing and normalization fingerprinting rather than tokens.
- Cache storage cost vs hit rate: persistent cache sizing needs capacity planning. Consider sharding by tokenizer-version and hot-key replication constraints.

Action items (next steps):

- Prototype: build a minimal TokenAdapter that returns IR and supports a simple LRU in-memory cache. (Owner: Maya)
- Instrumentation: add metrics hooks in adapter and runtime to capture timings for IR generation, IR->tokens conversion and sync fallback. (Owner: Ethan)
- Offline evaluation: run dataset of 10k recent short requests to estimate compressibility and IR reuse rate across top-5 tokenizers. (Owner: Priya)
- Design doc PR: draft a runtime integration spec with exact API shapes and fallbacks for the serving scheduler (Owner: Jordan).

Notes to reviewers:

- This is intentionally a sketch. The aim is to surface the operational tradeoffs and a minimal-contract API that the rest of the runtime can use without a heavy refactor. Focus feedback on the chosen IR shape, cache invalidation semantics, and scheduling knobs.

Quick timeline suggestion:

- 2 weeks: prototype + basic metrics on small canary traffic
- 4–6 weeks: persistent cache & prioritized scheduling experiments
- 8–12 weeks: iterative rollout into more traffic with auto-disable thresholds

References and similar prior work:

- Related internal: microbatch-kv-cache-eviction-handoff-spec (see historical notes for eviction strategies).
- External idea similarity: upstream model-serving projects that split normalization and byte-level token span detection from full token id generation.
